newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - EMAP says EGM will clear air.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - EMAP says EGM will clear air.

text.p: An extraordinary general meeting next month should end a boardroom row at UK media group EMAP and allow directors to refocus their attention on running the company, finance director David Grigson said on Monday.
"The EGM will be a purging process. It will clear the air and leave us with a smaller and happier board," Grigson told Reuters in a telephone interview.

"It will leave us with a board we all feel is capable of going on to better things," he said, dismissing suggestions that the row could see either chief executive Robin Miller or managing director David Arculus leave the company.
The EGM, scheduled for December 2, has been called to seek the removal of rebel non-executive directors Ken Simmonds and Joe Cooke from the board.

The pair oppose changes made to the company's articles at its annual general meeting in July. The new provisions removed a requirement for the company to have at least five non-executive directors and introduced a rule whereby a director could be ousted if 75 percent of the board voted for his removal.
The row has primarily pitted Simmonds and Cooke against chairman Sir John Hoskyns but some analysts feared that the divisions in the boardroom were more widespread.

Grigson said that profits had been boosted by a strong performance in the UK from the consumer magazines and commercial radio operations where advertising revenues grew by 10 percent and 25 percent respectively.
EMAP was bullish about its outlook, saying it was optimistic about the prospects for the second half and looked forward to a further sustained period of profit growth.
Grigson said that the outlook for the French economy -- EMAP's second main market -- was less rosy than the UK.
EMAP has a 16 percent share of the French consumer magazine market following its recent acqusition of Tele Star S.A.

Grigson said that EMAP continued to be on the look-out for suitable acquisitions. He said that the company would initially look at possible targets in Britain and France but could seek to expand in Germany and the United States.
